newsitem.title: USA: Singer reports loss, to exit U.S. furniture making.
newsitem.headline: Singer reports loss, to exit U.S. furniture making.

text.p: Singer Co. on Friday reported a surprising fourth-quarter loss of $20 million, its first since the company went public in 1991, and its stock plunged more than 20 percent.
Singer, best known for its sewing machines, also announced it was getting out of the furniture manufacturing business in the United States, which it blamed for much of the losses.
Its stock was the biggest loser in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, falling $4.625 to $17.
The fourth-quarter loss, equal to 39 cents per share, contrasted with a profit of $34.3 million, or 66 cents a share, in fourth-quarter 1995.
Fourth-quarter revenues slipped to $326.6 million from $387.2 million in the year-ago period.
"This is the the first quarter the company has reported a loss since going public in 1991," Singer Chairman James Ting said in a statement.
For the year, Singer had net income of $29 million, or 56 cents a share, vs. $84.4 million, or $1.64 per share, in 1995.
Annual revenues grew 7 percent to $1.307 billion from $1.223 billion in the previous year.

The company said it suffered a fourth-quarter loss of $16.5 million related to inefficiencies in cutting back its furniture manufacturing operations. Singer also said its Singer Furniture unit suffered from declining market share and considerable excess manufacturing capacity.

The company, which acquired the furniture company in 1995 as a result of a court ruling, said it closed two of its three furniture plants late last year and is starting talks to sell the remaining plant.
A Singer spokesman said the company would record no further costs for the furniture business
He said the company would continue making furniture in Latin America and Asia.
Singer attributed a large part of the fourth-quarter losses to a rise in labour costs following a costly two-week strike in Brazil.

"The unusual events of the last year, in particular the strike in Brazil and the withdrawal from the furniture businesses in the U.S., had a significant impact on earnings," Ting said. "The company believes it has taken the necessary corrective actions to restore its operations to their normal levels."
